content: Buckthorns, belonging to the genus Rhamnus (or two genera if Frangula is considered distinct), consist of approximately 100 species of shrubs or small trees. These plants typically range in height from 1 to 10 meters, though some species can grow up to 15 meters. They are members of the family Rhamnaceae. Buckthorns are native to temperate and subtropical regions of the Northern Hemisphere and are also found in localized areas of the subtropical Southern Hemisphere, including parts of Africa and South America. Both deciduous and evergreen species exist within this genus. The leaves of buckthorns are simple, measuring 3 to 15 cm in length, and are arranged either alternately or in opposite pairs. A notable feature of many buckthorn species is the upward curving venation of the leaves, which extends toward the leaf tip. The plants produce dark blue berries as their fruit. The name buckthorn originates from the presence of a woody spine at the end of each twig in many species. Buckthorns serve as food plants for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, which are moths and butterflies. These interactions are documented in lists of Lepidoptera that feed on buckthorns. Classification The genus Rhamnus is divided into two subgenera, which are sometimes treated as separate genera: 1. Subgenus Rhamnus: Flowers have four petals. Buds are covered with bud scales. Leaves can be either opposite or alternate. Branches often have spines. Examples include: Rhamnus alaternus (Italian Buckthorn) Rhamnus alnifolia (Alderleaf Buckthorn) Rhamnus arguta (Sharp-tooth Buckthorn) Rhamnus cathartica (Common or Purging Buckthorn) Rhamnus crocea (Redberry Buckthorn, Hollyleaf Buckthorn) Rhamnus davurica (Dahurian Buckthorn) Rhamnus globosa (Lokao Buckthorn) Rhamnus ilicifolia (Hollyleaf Redberry) Rhamnus japonica (Japanese Buckthorn) Rhamnus lanceolata (Lanceleaf Buckthorn) Rhamnus saxatilis (Rock Buckthorn, Avignon Buckthorn) Rhamnus utilis (Chinese Buckthorn) 2. Subgenus Frangula: Flowers have five petals. Buds lack bud scales. Leaves are always alternate. Branches lack spines. Examples include: Rhamnus betulaefolia (Frangula betulifolia, Birchleaf Buckthorn) Rhamnus californica (Frangula californica, California Buckthorn or Coffeeberry) Rhamnus caroliniana (Frangula caroliniana, Carolina Buckthorn or Indian Cherry) Rhamnus frangula (Frangula alnus, Alder Buckthorn or Glossy Buckthorn) Rhamnus purshiana (Frangula purshiana, Cascara Buckthorn) Notable Species and Uses The Common Buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica), native to Europe, was historically used as a purgative. However, its toxicity makes it a dangerous herbal remedy, and it is no longer used medicinally. Introduced to the United States as a garden shrub, it has become an invasive species in many areas. It is also a primary host for the soybean aphid (Aphis glycines), a significant pest for soybean farmers. The aphids overwinter on buckthorn and spread to soybean fields in the spring. The Alder Buckthorn (Rhamnus frangula, Frangula alnus) was historically important for producing high-quality charcoal used in gunpowder manufacturing from the 15th to 19th centuries. The Italian Buckthorn (Rhamnus alaternus), an evergreen species from the Mediterranean, has become a problematic weed in parts of New Zealand, particularly on the Hauraki Gulf islands. The Dyer's Buckthorn (Rhamnus tinctoria) and the Chinese Buckthorn (Rhamnus utilis) are used to produce the dye China green. The Avignon Buckthorn (Rhamnus saxatilis) provides the yellow dye known as Persian berry, derived from its berries. Rhamnus glandulosa (Sanguinho) is endemic to the Macaronesian islands, where it grows in the laurel forests of Madeira and the Canary Islands. Geographic Distribution In North America, notable species include: Rhamnus alnifolia (Alderleaf Buckthorn) across the continent. Rhamnus caroliniana (Frangula caroliniana, Carolina Buckthorn) in the eastern regions. Rhamnus purshiana (Frangula purshiana, Cascara Buckthorn) in the west. Rhamnus californica (Frangula californica, California Buckthorn or Coffeeberry) and Rhamnus crocea (Hollyleaf Buckthorn) in the west. In South America, Rhamnus diffusus is a small shrub native to the Valdivian temperate rainforests of Chile. Differentiation from Dogwoods Buckthorns can be confused with dogwoods due to their similar curved leaf venation. However, they can be distinguished by slowly pulling a leaf apart. Dogwoods exude thin white latex strings, which are absent in buckthorns. In southern Africa, Rhamnus prinoides is locally referred to as dogwood and is used to make Ethiopian mead, known as gesho in Ethiopia.
